description: A team of three tech enthusiast people from St. Xavier's College, Maitighar.
summary: Koshi Watch is an interactive environmental observatory that combines satellite imagery, historical water data, rainfall and modelled river discharge to visualise changes in the Sapta Koshi River across eastern Nepal and northern Bihar, India. Using observations from Sentinel II, JRC channel, Landsat and NASA MODIS  and other environmental datasets, it allows users to compare river pathways and investigate changes in surrounding wetlands and water distribution, with historical satellite coverage extending back to 1988. Although the Koshi River's historical migration, reportedly spanning over 113 kilometres across its megafan, is well documented, understanding these changes through written records alone can be difficult. Furthermore, relevant environmental data is freely available but scattered across multiple platforms, making it challenging to access and compare. Koshi Watch addresses these problems by bringing diverse datasets together in one interactive map, transforming complex scientific information into accessible visualisations. Our goal is to make environmental knowledge easier to understand, encourage interest in Earth observation and help more people engage with the changing landscape of the Koshi River basin.
details:
Koshi Watch

Koshi Watch is an interactive environmental observatory designed to visualise and analyse changes in the Sapta Koshi River basin across eastern Nepal and northern Bihar, India. It brings together satellite imagery, river-channel changes, historical surface-water occurrence, rainfall data and modelled river discharge into a single platform. By combining these datasets, the application makes complex environmental information easier to explore, compare and understand.

About the Koshi River:

The Koshi River is one of the most dynamic river systems in South Asia. Historical records indicate that its channel migrated approximately 113 kilometres across its megafan over the last two centuries. However, research by Chakraborty et al. (2010) suggests that this movement was oscillatory rather than continuously westward. Such changes are important because they influence surrounding landscapes, wetlands, agricultural areas, settlements and ecosystems. Despite the availability of satellite observations and environmental datasets, understanding these changes often requires specialised technical knowledge and access to multiple disconnected platforms. This creates an accessibility gap between the availability of environmental information and people's ability to interpret it.

What our project does:

Koshi Watch addresses this problem through an interactive, map-based interface that allows users to explore environmental changes across four important study areas: Koshi Tappu, Koshi Barrage, the Kusaha breach corridor and the Chatara gorge. Users can compare satellite observations from different dates, examine historical river pathways, explore wetland changes and investigate rainfall and modelled discharge patterns. The application also includes a Normalised Difference Water Index (NDWI)-based feature that estimates surface-water coverage from optical satellite imagery within selected study areas. These features allow users to investigate how the river and its surrounding environment have changed over time without needing to work directly with complicated scientific datasets.

Datasets and Resources:

The application integrates several freely available Earth observation and environmental datasets. These include Copernicus Sentinel-2, United States Geological Survey Landsat Collection 2, Sentinel-1, NASA Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) and NASA-ISRO NISAR, alongside the European Commission Joint Research Centre's Global Surface Water datasets. It also incorporates Copernicus Global Flood Awareness System discharge data and European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts ERA5 rainfall reanalysis. Landsat observations provide historical coverage extending back to 1988, while newer satellite missions offer additional and complementary observations. Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) imagery is particularly useful because it can observe the Earth's surface through cloud cover, complementing optical imagery when atmospheric conditions limit visibility.

Development Details:

The project was developed using Python and Flask for the backend, alongside browser-based frontend technologies for the interactive interface. We used geospatial analysis, remote sensing techniques, image processing and mapping technologies to integrate and visualise the different datasets. The application retrieves information from upstream data providers and processes and displays it according to the user's selected location, date and dataset. This approach allows multiple environmental information sources to be explored through one platform instead of requiring users to navigate between separate services.

What sets our project apart:

What makes Koshi Watch creative is its approach to combining scattered scientific datasets into a single, accessible environmental observatory focused on a geographically significant transboundary river system. Rather than simply displaying satellite images, the platform allows users to compare different types of observations and explore how various environmental indicators relate to one another. Its focus on the Koshi basin also gives users a way to investigate a river system that has significant environmental and geographical importance to both Nepal and India. By transforming information that would otherwise require specialised software and expertise into interactive visualisations, the project makes Earth observation more approachable for students, researchers, communities and environmental enthusiasts.

Throughout development, our team considered several factors, including data accessibility, scientific reliability, geographical coverage, image resolution, historical availability and usability. We also considered the limitations of satellite observations, such as cloud contamination, acquisition frequency, mixed pixels and differences between satellite sensors. We recognised that satellite-derived measurements and modelled estimates are not equivalent to direct field observations. Therefore, Koshi Watch is designed as an exploratory environmental observatory rather than an operational flood forecasting or warning system. Its visualisations help users investigate environmental patterns but are not intended to replace official warnings or ground-based measurements.

Conclusion:

The intended impact of Koshi Watch is to make environmental knowledge more accessible, encourage interest in Earth observation and climate research, and improve public awareness of changes occurring within the Koshi River basin. It can help students understand geographical processes, support researchers exploring historical environmental patterns and allow interested communities to engage with satellite-based information. More broadly, the project demonstrates how publicly available scientific datasets can be transformed into useful tools for understanding environmental change.

We believe that environmental changes should not remain hidden behind complicated datasets and specialised software. By making these changes visible, comparable and understandable, Koshi Watch aims to bring environmental science closer to the people and communities it affects.

References:

  1. Chakraborty, T., Kar, R., Ghosh, P., & Basu, S. (2010). Kosi megafan: Historical records, geomorphology and the recent avulsion of the Kosi River. Quaternary International, 227(2), 143–160. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.quaint.2009.12.002
